intro: Your body works hard every day. It runs, thinks, grows and plays. In this unit you will learn how to help it. You will learn about germs and how clean hands keep them away.
You will also learn what gives your body energy. Food, water, sleep and play all help. Every body is different, and that is okay. At the end, you will be able to plan a healthy day for yourself.
bigQuestion: What can I do each day to keep my body healthy?

timeline.t: Wake up after about 10 hours of sleep
Brush your teeth for about two minutes
Wash your hands and eat a good breakfast
Cough or sneeze into your elbow at school
Warm up, then move and play at recess
Rest and drink water when you feel tired
Scrub with soap for 20 seconds before dinner
Take a bath, brush your teeth and read a book
Go to bed at the same time each night

words.d: tiny living things too small to see with just your eyes
a tool that makes tiny things look big
something you rub on your skin that lifts off germs and dirt
a soft paper you use to wipe your nose
holes in teeth that germs can make
the power your body uses to move, think and grow
the same calm steps you do each night before sleep
parts of your body that help you move

test.why: Germs are tiny living things too small to see.

test.q: How long should you scrub your hands with soap?
test.why: Scrub for about 20 seconds, like two Happy Birthday songs.

test.q: Where should you sneeze if you have no tissue?
test.why: Your elbow does not touch toys or friends.

test.q: Why should you keep your own cup when you are sick?
choices: So germs do not go to friends
test.why: Germs from your mouth get on the cup.

test.q: What can germs on your teeth make?
test.why: Germs eat food on teeth and can make cavities.
Food is fuel. It gives you energy.
Chips are a treat to enjoy now and then.

test.q: About how much sleep do many kids need each night?
test.why: Many kids need about 10 hours of sleep.

test.q: What should you do before hard play?
test.why: A warm up gets your body ready to play.

test.q: Omar uses a wheelchair and Lily runs. What is true?
choices: Every body is different, and that is okay
test.why: Each body moves in its own way.

write.prompt: What is one thing you can do tomorrow to stay healthy? Tell or draw your idea. Use two facts from this unit to say why it helps.
tips: Pick one thing, like washing hands or going to bed on time.
Use a word from the unit, like germs or energy.
Say why it helps your body.
You can draw, say or write your idea.

title: My Healthy Body

chapters.title: Germs and Clean Hands
chapters.bigQuestion: How can we keep germs from making us and our friends sick?

story.title: The Glitter Hands
story.kicker: Leo's teacher puts glitter on one hand. Soon the glitter is everywhere.
paragraphs: It is Monday in Ms. Reyes's class. She holds up a jar of gold glitter. "Leo, hold out your hand," she says. She shakes a little glitter on his palm. Leo smiles. His hand sparkles.
"Now say good morning to your friends," Ms. Reyes says. Leo shakes hands with Maya. He gives Sam a high five. He picks up a crayon. He opens the door for Ana.
Soon Maya's hand sparkles. Sam's hand sparkles too. The crayon is gold. The door handle is gold. Leo only had glitter on one hand. Now it is all over the room!
"Germs spread the same way," Ms. Reyes says. "But germs are too small to see." Then the class washes with soap and water. They scrub and scrub. The glitter goes down the drain.
story.think: The glitter moved from hand to hand. What are some things your hands touch every day?

lessons.title: Tiny Living Things
lessons.mainIdea: Germs are tiny living things that are too small to see.
reading: Look at your hand. It looks clean. But tiny things live on it. They are called *germs*. They are so small you cannot see them with just your eyes.
Scientists look at germs with a *microscope*. A microscope makes tiny things look big. Then they can see germs. Germs are alive. They can grow and make more germs.

words.d: tiny living things too small to see with just your eyes
a tool that makes tiny things look big

look.title: A Drop of Pond Water
look.text: Look at a drop of pond water on a glass slide. It looks clear. Now look at it with a microscope. Tiny living things wiggle and swim. You could not see them before.
look.prompt: Why could you see the tiny things only with the microscope?

check.q: What are germs?
check.why: Germs are tiny living things. They are too small to see with just your eyes.

check.q: Why can't we see germs on our hands?
choices: They only come out at night
check.why: Germs are too small to see with just our eyes.

check.q: What tool helps us see germs?
check.why: A microscope makes tiny things look big.

lessons.title: Some Germs Make Us Sick
lessons.mainIdea: Most germs do not hurt us, but some germs can make us sick.
reading: Germs live almost everywhere. They live in dirt, on toys and in your body. Many germs do not hurt you. Some even help you. Germs in your belly help you use your food.
But some germs can make you sick. A cold comes from a germ. So does the flu. These germs can get into your body. They can get in through your nose, mouth or eyes.

words.d: not feeling well in your body

look.title: Sam Has a Cold
look.text: Look at Sam. His nose is runny. He sneezes. He feels tired. A germ got into his body. Now his body is working hard to fight it. Sam rests at home and drinks water.
look.prompt: How did the germ get into Sam's body? Name one way.

check.q: Do all germs make us sick?
choices: Yes, every germ makes us sick
No, many germs do not hurt us
check.why: Many germs do not hurt us. Some even help us.

check.q: Where do germs in your belly help?
check.why: Germs in your belly help your body use food.

check.q: How can a germ get into your body?
check.why: Germs can get in through your nose, mouth or eyes.

lessons.title: Soap and Water
lessons.mainIdea: Washing with soap and water takes germs off your hands.
reading: Your hands touch lots of things. They touch doors, toys and tables. Germs get on your hands. Then you touch your mouth or eyes. The germs can get in.
*Soap* helps. Soap lifts germs and dirt off your skin. Water rinses them away. Water alone does not work as well. Use soap and water together.
Wash your hands before you eat. Wash after you use the toilet. Wash after you blow your nose. Wash when you come in from play.

words.d: something you rub on your skin that lifts off germs and dirt

look.title: Maya's Snack Time
look.text: Look at Maya. She just played in the sandbox. Now it is snack time. Her apple slices sit on the table. Maya walks to the sink first. She turns on the water and gets soap.
look.prompt: Why does Maya wash before she eats her apple?

check.q: What does soap do?
choices: It lifts germs off your skin
check.why: Soap lifts germs and dirt off your skin.

check.q: When should you wash your hands?
check.why: Wash before you eat, after the toilet and after you blow your nose.

check.q: Which works best to clean hands?
check.why: Soap lifts the germs. Water rinses them away.

lessons.title: Scrub for 20 Seconds
lessons.mainIdea: Scrub your hands with soap for about 20 seconds, as long as a short song.
reading: Germs hold on tight. A quick splash does not get them off. You need to *scrub*. Rub your hands together with soap. Rub the backs. Rub between your fingers. Rub under your nails.
Scrub for about 20 seconds. That is how long doctors say to wash. How long is 20 seconds? Hum the Happy Birthday song two times. Then rinse and dry your hands.

words.d: to rub hard to get something clean

look.title: Steps to Wash Your Hands
look.cite: CDC, When and How to Wash Your Hands, 2024
look.prompt: What step comes right after you put on soap?

check.q: How long should you scrub with soap?
check.why: Doctors say to scrub for about 20 seconds.

check.q: What can help you scrub long enough?
check.why: Humming Happy Birthday two times takes about 20 seconds.

check.q: Where should you scrub?
choices: Backs, between fingers and under nails
check.why: Germs hide in many places. Scrub the backs, between fingers and under nails.

lessons.title: Cough Into Your Elbow
lessons.mainIdea: Cough or sneeze into a tissue or your elbow to keep germs off others.
reading: A sneeze sends out tiny drops. The drops can carry germs. They can fly far. They land on people and things around you.
You can stop them. Use a *tissue*. Then throw it away and wash your hands. No tissue? Cough or sneeze into your *elbow*. Your elbow does not touch toys or friends.

words.d: a soft paper you use to wipe your nose
the bend in the middle of your arm

look.title: Ana Feels a Sneeze
look.text: Look at Ana at her desk. Her nose tickles. A sneeze is coming. There is no tissue on her desk. Ana turns her head. She lifts her arm and sneezes into the bend of her arm.
look.prompt: Why did Ana sneeze into her elbow and not her hand?

check.q: What can a sneeze carry?
check.why: A sneeze sends out tiny drops. The drops can carry germs.

check.q: No tissue? Where should you sneeze?
check.why: Your elbow does not touch toys or friends.

check.q: What do you do after you use a tissue?
choices: Throw it away and wash hands
check.why: Throw the tissue away. Then wash your hands.

lessons.title: Brush and Bathe
lessons.mainIdea: Brushing teeth twice a day and taking baths keep your body clean.
reading: Germs live in your mouth too. Some germs eat bits of food on your teeth. They can make holes called *cavities*. Brushing takes the food and germs away.
Brush your teeth two times a day. Brush in the morning. Brush at night before bed. Brush for about two minutes. A grown-up can help you.
Baths and showers help too. Soap and water wash germs and sweat off your whole body. You feel fresh and clean.

words.d: holes in teeth that germs can make

look.title: Brushing Your Teeth
look.cite: American Dental Association, Brushing Your Teeth, MouthHealthy.org
look.prompt: How many times do you brush in one whole day?

check.q: How many times a day should you brush your teeth?
check.why: Brush two times a day, in the morning and at night.

check.q: What can germs in your mouth make?
check.why: Germs eat food on teeth and can make holes called cavities.

check.q: What does a bath wash off?
check.why: Soap and water wash germs and sweat off your body.

lessons.title: Keep Your Own Cup
lessons.mainIdea: When someone is sick, do not share cups, spoons or straws.
reading: Your mouth has germs. When you drink, some germs get on the cup. If a friend drinks next, the germs go to them.
Use your own cup. Use your own spoon and straw. This matters most when someone is sick. Sharing is kind. But keep your cup to yourself. That is kind too.

words.d: to let someone else use something of yours

look.title: Two Water Bottles
look.text: Look at the lunch table. Sam has a red water bottle. Leo has a blue one. Sam has a cold today. Leo is thirsty and asks for a sip from the red bottle. Sam holds it close. "Use your blue one," he says.

check.q: How do germs get from one cup to a friend?
choices: The friend drinks from the same cup
The cup is the wrong color
The friend looks at the cup
check.why: Germs from your mouth get on the cup. The next person drinks them.

check.q: When does keeping your own cup matter most?
check.why: Not sharing cups matters most when someone is sick.

check.q: Which is a kind choice when you have a cold?
check.why: Keeping your own cup keeps germs away from friends.

review.q: In the story, what did the glitter show?
review.why: The glitter went from hand to hand, just like germs do.

review.q: Why do we need a microscope to see germs?
review.why: Germs are too small to see with just our eyes.

review.q: What is the best way to clean your hands?
review.why: Soap and water take germs off your hands.

review.q: How long should you scrub your hands?
review.why: Scrub for about 20 seconds, or two Happy Birthday songs.

review.q: Leo has no tissue. He needs to cough. What should he do?
review.why: Coughing into your elbow keeps germs off hands and friends.

review.q: How often should you brush your teeth?
review.why: Brush in the morning and at night.

chapters.title: Food, Sleep and Play
chapters.bigQuestion: What does my body need to have energy for my day?

story.title: The Late Night Before the Game
story.kicker: Rosa stays up late. The next day, soccer feels very hard.
paragraphs: It is Friday night. Rosa has a soccer game in the morning. But there is a movie on TV. Rosa wants to see the end. She stays up late. She goes to bed long after her bedtime.
In the morning, Rosa's eyes feel heavy. She yawns and yawns. She is in a hurry, so she skips breakfast. Her mom hands her a water bottle. They drive to the field.
The game starts. Rosa runs after the ball. Her legs feel slow. She misses an easy kick. She feels grumpy. Her friend Kim runs fast and scores. Kim went to bed on time and ate eggs and toast.
After the game, Rosa sits on the grass. "I felt so tired," she tells her coach. The coach smiles. "Your body needs sleep and food to play," he says. "Let's try again next week."
story.think: Why do you think Kim had more energy than Rosa?

lessons.title: Food Is Fuel
lessons.mainIdea: Food gives your body the energy it needs to move, think and grow.
reading: A car needs gas to go. Your body needs food to go. Food gives you *energy*. Energy lets you run, jump, think and grow.
When you skip a meal, you may feel slow or grumpy. A good breakfast helps you start the day. It helps you learn and play at school.

words.d: the power your body uses to move, think and grow

look.title: Two Mornings
look.text: Look at two mornings. On Monday, Jay eats oatmeal and a banana. He runs at recess and listens well in class. On Tuesday, Jay skips breakfast. By ten o'clock his tummy rumbles and he feels slow.
look.prompt: Which morning gave Jay more energy? How can you tell?

check.q: What does food give your body?
check.why: Food gives you energy to move, think and grow.

check.q: How might you feel if you skip breakfast?
check.why: Skipping a meal can make you feel slow or grumpy.

check.q: A car needs gas. What does your body need?
check.why: Food is fuel for your body, like gas for a car.

lessons.title: Many Kinds of Food
lessons.mainIdea: Eat many kinds of food: fruits, vegetables, grains, protein and milk foods.
reading: Food comes in groups. *Fruits* like apples and berries. Vegetables like carrots and peas. *Grains* like bread, rice and oatmeal. Protein like beans, eggs, fish and meat. Milk foods like milk, yogurt and cheese.
Each group helps your body in its own way. So eat many colors and kinds. Try to fill half your plate with fruits and vegetables.

words.d: sweet foods that grow on plants, like apples and berries
foods made from seeds like wheat or rice, such as bread

look.title: A Healthy Plate
look.prompt: Name one food from each of the five groups.

check.q: Which food is a grain?
check.why: Rice is a grain, like bread and oatmeal.

check.q: How much of your plate should be fruits and vegetables?
check.why: Try to fill half your plate with fruits and vegetables.

check.q: Which food is protein?
check.why: Beans are protein, like eggs, fish and meat.

lessons.title: Water and Sometimes Foods
lessons.mainIdea: Water is the best drink, and sweets are sometimes foods.
reading: Your body is made of lots of water. You lose water when you sweat and play. So drink water every day. Water is the best drink when you are thirsty.
Candy, chips and soda taste good. They are *sometimes foods*. You can enjoy them now and then. But they do not give your body all it needs to grow.

words.d: treats like candy and chips to enjoy only now and then

look.title: After Recess
look.text: Look at the class after a hot recess. Faces are red. Everyone is thirsty. On the table is a pitcher of cold water and a can of soda. Mia picks up a cup and fills it with water.
look.prompt: Why is water a good choice for Mia after playing?

check.q: What is the best drink when you are thirsty?
check.why: Water is the best drink when you are thirsty.

check.q: Which is a sometimes food?
check.why: Candy is a treat to enjoy now and then.

check.q: When do you lose water?
check.why: You lose water when you sweat and play.

lessons.title: Why We Sleep
lessons.mainIdea: Sleep helps your body grow and rest, and helps your brain learn.
reading: At night you close your eyes. You sleep. But your body is busy. It grows. It fixes small hurts. Your brain sorts out what you learned that day.
When you do not get enough sleep, you feel tired. It is hard to pay attention. You may feel grumpy, like Rosa. Sleep gives you a fresh start.

words.d: the time your body and brain rest at night

look.title: Rosa's Two Games
look.text: Look back at Rosa. She stayed up late and her legs felt slow in the game. The next Friday she goes to bed on time. On Saturday she runs fast. She kicks the ball and smiles.
look.prompt: What changed for Rosa the second time?

check.q: What does your body do while you sleep?
check.why: While you sleep, your body grows and fixes small hurts.

check.q: What does your brain do while you sleep?
choices: It sorts out what you learned
check.why: Your brain sorts out what you learned that day.

check.q: How might you feel without enough sleep?
check.why: Too little sleep can make you tired and grumpy.

lessons.title: How Much Sleep?
lessons.mainIdea: Children your age need about 10 hours of sleep each night.
reading: Kids need more sleep than grown-ups. Children in school need about 9 to 12 hours each night. Many need about 10 hours.
A *bedtime routine* helps. Take a bath. Brush your teeth. Read a book. Turn off screens. Go to bed at the same time each night.

words.d: the same calm steps you do each night before sleep

look.title: Hours of Sleep Each Night
look.cite: American Academy of Sleep Medicine, Paruthi and others, 2016; CDC
look.prompt: Who needs more sleep, children or grown-ups?

check.q: About how much sleep do many kids need?
check.why: Children in school need about 9 to 12 hours. Many need about 10.

check.q: Who needs more sleep?
check.why: Kids need more sleep than grown-ups.

check.q: Which step fits a bedtime routine?
check.why: Reading a book is a calm step before sleep.

lessons.title: Move Every Day
lessons.mainIdea: Moving and playing every day makes your heart and muscles strong.
reading: Run, jump, dance, ride a bike. Moving is good for you. It makes your heart strong. It makes your *muscles* strong. It helps you feel happy too.
Doctors say kids should move and play about one hour every day. You can move in many ways. Before hard play, *warm up*. Walk or march slowly first. It gets your body ready.

words.d: parts of your body that help you move
to move slowly first to get your body ready for play

look.title: Moving Every Day
rows: Days a week for strong-muscle play
Days a week for strong-bone play
look.cite: CDC, Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd ed., 2018
look.prompt: How many minutes a day should kids move and play?

check.q: How long should kids move each day?
check.why: Doctors say kids should move about one hour every day.

check.q: What does moving make strong?
check.why: Moving makes your heart and muscles strong.

check.q: What should you do before hard play?
check.why: A warm up gets your body ready for play.

lessons.title: Rest When You Are Tired
lessons.mainIdea: Resting when you are tired helps your body get ready to play again.
reading: After you run, your heart beats fast. You breathe hard. That is okay. Your body is working. Now it is time to *rest*.
Sit down. Take slow breaths. Drink water. Listen to your body. When it says it is tired, you can take a break. A break is a smart choice.

words.d: to stop and let your body be still and calm

look.title: Tag at Recess
look.text: Look at Ben playing tag. He runs and runs. His face is warm. He breathes hard. Ben sits on the bench. He takes slow breaths and sips water. In a few minutes he jumps up to play again.
look.prompt: How did the rest help Ben?

check.q: What can you do when your body feels tired?
check.why: When your body is tired, you can take a break.

check.q: Which helps you rest?
check.why: Slow breaths and water help your body rest.

check.q: Why did Ben sit on the bench?
choices: He was tired and needed rest
check.why: Ben breathed hard, so he rested and then played again.

lessons.title: Every Body Is Different
lessons.mainIdea: Each body is different, and that is okay.
reading: Look around your class. Some kids are tall. Some are short. Some run fast. Some move in a wheelchair. Some like to dance. Some like to swim.
Every body is *different*. Each body grows in its own way and time. You can find the foods, sleep and play that help your body. Ask a parent, nurse or doctor what is best for you.

words.d: not the same as something else

look.title: Field Day
look.text: Look at field day. Omar races in his wheelchair. Lily hops in a sack. Theo throws a ball far. Grace walks the track with her friend. Everyone moves in their own way. Everyone cheers.
look.prompt: Name two different ways kids moved on field day.

check.q: Are all bodies the same?
choices: Yes, they are all the same
check.why: Every body is different, and that is okay.

check.q: Who can help you learn what is best for your body?
check.why: Ask a parent, nurse or doctor what is best for you.

check.q: How did Omar move on field day?
check.why: Omar raced in his wheelchair. Everyone moves in their own way.

review.q: Why did Rosa feel slow at her game?
choices: She stayed up late and skipped breakfast
review.why: Rosa did not get enough sleep or food, so she had less energy.

review.q: Which food group is yogurt in?
review.why: Yogurt is a milk food, like milk and cheese.

review.q: What is the best drink when you are thirsty?
About how long should kids move and play each day?
review.why: Kids should move about one hour every day.

review.q: What does a warm up do?
choices: Gets your body ready to play
review.why: A warm up gets your body ready before hard play.

choices: Every body is different, and that is okay
review.why: Each body grows and moves in its own way.
